theme: price-level reversion against a trailing reference
trace: The strategy aims to exploit mean-reverting behavior in stock prices around key price levels. The idea is to identify historical support and resistance levels for a stock or index. When the price deviates significantly from these levels, trades are placed in the direction opposite to the current trend. This mechanism might persist due to investor psychology and market inefficiencies. The rule would involve setting thresholds around identified levels; if prices fall below (or rise above) these thresholds, a buy (or sell) order is triggered, aiming to benefit from price reversion back towards the mean level.

The signal for this strategy involves identifying support and resistance levels through historical price data. For each stock or index, calculate the average high and low prices over a specified lookback period (e.g., 200 days). Define upper and lower thresholds around these mean levels based on standard deviations (e.g., ±1 standard deviation). On each trading day, compute whether the current price has deviated from its historical support or resistance level. Candidates for trades are ranked by their distance from the threshold levels; those closer to the thresholds trigger buy/sell signals, aiming to capture reversion towards the mean. Higher ranks indicate a stronger signal to enter the opposite position of the prevailing trend.

This strategy should be implemented with a diversified portfolio to spread risk. Hold up to 30-50 individual stocks or indices, ensuring no single security exceeds 5% of the total portfolio value. Positions can be equally weighted among selected candidates or adjusted based on relative strength and liquidity. Set stop-loss orders at ±2 standard deviations from the mean price levels to limit potential losses to approximately 4%-6% per position, maintaining a maximum overall loss of about 20%-30% across the entire portfolio. This approach balances exposure to mean-reverting behavior while managing risk effectively.
